title: VCP
teaches: The VCP (volatility contraction pattern) as we trade it: a leader in an uptrend pulls back in a run of swings that each get smaller, volume dries up into the tight final swing, the pivot is the high of that final swing, the buy is the trade through it at market in regular hours and no more than 4% past it, the stop sits a few cents under the entry day's low, a third comes off at 3R and 5R with the rest on the trail, and a loss at the stop is the system working.

questions.q: What does a VCP stand for?
choices: Volatility Contraction Pattern
Velocity Confirmation Pattern
Volume Compression Pivot Pattern
questions.why: Volatility Contraction Pattern. Minervini wants the stock to move from greater volatility on the left side of the base to lesser volatility on the right.
questions.lesson_line: A VCP is a base whose price swings shrink from left to right.

wrong.Volume Compression Pivot Pattern: Volume matters, but the name is about the size of the price swings.
wrong.Velocity Confirmation Pattern: No such pattern. The name describes swings that contract.

questions.q: In a VCP, the price swings get smaller from the left side of the base to the right side.
questions.why: True. Minervini wants greater volatility on the left side of the price base and lesser volatility on the right.
questions.lesson_line: Left side wide, right side tight. The swings contract.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Each pullback in a VCP is ___ than the one before it.
questions.why: Smaller. Each successive pullback in a VCP is smaller than the one before. A wiggle that does not shrink is not a VCP.
questions.lesson_line: Every pullback in a VCP is smaller than the last.

questions.q: What is the pivot of a VCP?
choices: The low of the first pullback
The 200-day average
The high of the final contraction
The highest price of the whole base
questions.answer: The high of the final contraction
questions.why: The high of the final contraction. It is the level the last tight stretch keeps running into, not the highest price of the whole base.
questions.lesson_line: The pivot is the top of the last, tightest swing.

wrong.The highest price of the whole base: The pivot may sit below the base's high. The last swing's high is the level to clear.
wrong.The low of the first pullback: That is the bottom of the deepest swing, far from the breakout level.
wrong.The 200-day average: An average is a trend check. The pivot is a price level in the base.

questions.q: A VCP's pivot may sit below the highest high of the base.
questions.why: True. The pivot is the high of the final contraction, and it may sit below the base's left-side high.
questions.lesson_line: The pivot is the last swing's high, even when the base high is higher.

questions.q: The buy is a market order, placed once price trades through the pivot in regular hours.
questions.why: True. Entries are market orders, and there are no new buys outside regular hours.
questions.lesson_line: Trade through the pivot, regular hours, market order.

questions.q: Where does the stop go on a VCP breakout?
choices: Exactly on the day's low
At the 50-day average
At the low of the first pullback
A few cents under the day's low
questions.answer: A few cents under the day's low
questions.why: A few cents under the day's low, by default. The stop comes first and the size comes from it.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the day's low, then size from the stop.

wrong.At the low of the first pullback: That can be far away. Widening the stop to give the stock room is a named mistake.
wrong.At the 50-day average: An average is a trend check, not our stop.
wrong.Exactly on the day's low: A stop exactly on the low is hit by the first wiggle. We sit a few cents under it.

questions.q: A VCP is a pause inside a prior uptrend, not a base in a downtrend.
questions.why: True. Minervini looks for consolidations that are pauses within the context of a prior uptrend, and he never goes against the long-term trend.
questions.lesson_line: The base sits inside an uptrend. A tight base in a downtrend does not qualify.

questions.q: Which trend does a VCP belong in?
choices: A Stage 2 uptrend
A Stage 4 downtrend
A sideways drift under the 200-day
questions.why: A Stage 2 uptrend. Minervini goes long a Stage 2 uptrend and never against the long-term trend.
questions.lesson_line: Long VCPs belong in uptrends. Check the trend before the box.

wrong.A Stage 4 downtrend: Minervini goes short a Stage 4 downtrend. A long VCP does not belong there.
wrong.A sideways drift under the 200-day: Below the 200-day we do not buy. The long needs a trend under it.

questions.q: A perfect VCP in a Red market is still a buy.
questions.why: False. In a Red market there are no VCP buys. ChartMill: in a negative market even perfect VCPs fail en masse.
questions.lesson_line: Red market: no VCP buys. Even perfect bases fail when buyers are missing.

questions.q: What RS rating do we want from a VCP leader?
choices: 80 or more
70, Minervini's floor
50, the middle of the market
questions.why: 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. Minervini's floor is 70, and the house rule is higher.
questions.lesson_line: We buy leaders: RS 80 or more in a strong group.

wrong.70, Minervini's floor: That is Minervini's floor. Our rule asks for more.
wrong.50, the middle of the market: A middling stock is not a leader. We buy the strongest.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A long VCP needs price above the ___-day average.
questions.why: 200. No longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long.
questions.lesson_line: No longs under the 200-day. A VCP has to pass that first.

questions.q: If the pullbacks in a base stop shrinking, it is not a VCP.
questions.why: True. A contraction as deep as, or deeper than, the one before ends the VCP idea. The contractions must shrink.
questions.lesson_line: No shrinking, no VCP. A wide and loose base waits.

questions.q: Which floor applies to a VCP we buy?
choices: $5 a share and $5 million a day
$10 a share and $20 million a day
No floor if the base is tight
questions.answer: $10 a share and $20 million a day
questions.why: $10 a share and $20 million a day. The floor is the same for every setup.
questions.lesson_line: Thin, cheap stocks are off the list however tight the chart.

wrong.No floor if the base is tight: A tight chart on a thin stock is still a pass.

questions.q: The first pullback is 24%. Each next one is half the last. How deep is the third?
questions.why: 6. Halve the 24% twice. Minervini likes each contraction at about half the previous one.
questions.lesson_line: About half each time. The swings shrink fast.

questions.q: The final contraction's high is 170.00 and its low is 164.05. How deep is it, in percent?
questions.why: 3.5. The final contraction fell 3.5% from its high. ChartMill wants it under 10%, and the closer to 3% to 6%, the better.
questions.lesson_line: Depth is high minus low, divided by the high. The last swing should be the tightest.

questions.q: Fill 170.00, stop 165.39. How far under the fill is the stop, in percent?
questions.why: 2.7. The stop is 2.7% under the fill. Our stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the stop in percent before you size the trade.

questions.q: Bought at 17.38 with the stop at 16.59. Where is 3R?
questions.why: 19.75. One R is the fill minus the stop. Add three of those to the fill. PHM reached it in 16 days.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. The first third comes off there.

questions.q: The pivot is 16.47. What is the most we would pay under the 4% chase limit?
questions.why: 17.13. Add 4% to the pivot. Above that the stop distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: Know the chase limit before the open: 4% over the pivot.

questions.q: What is your move?
choices: Buy half now and the rest on a dip
Buy it now; the volume is heavy
Pass; more than 4% past the pivot
questions.answer: Pass; more than 4% past the pivot
questions.why: Pass. 17.40 is more than 4% above 16.47. When you find it already past 4%, it is a skip.
questions.lesson_line: Past 4% over the pivot you are chasing. Wait for the next setup.

wrong.Buy it now; the volume is heavy: Heavy volume does not lift the 4% limit.
wrong.Buy half now and the rest on a dip: We do not scale in. One full buy, one stop.

questions.story: A VCP's pivot is 16.47. You find the stock trading at 17.40 on heavy volume.

questions.q: In a VCP the final contraction should be the tightest swing of the base.
questions.why: True. ChartMill calls the final contraction the most important one, and it has to be tight. Under 10% is ideal.
questions.lesson_line: The last swing is the tightest, and it sets the pivot.

questions.q: How should volume look in the final contraction?
choices: Spiking on a wide, heavy down day
Drying up, below the 50-day average
Rising, above the 50-day average
questions.why: Drying up, below the 50-day average. The final contraction's average volume is also below the first contraction's.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet price, quiet volume. Supply is gone before the breakout.

wrong.Rising, above the 50-day average: Rising volume in a tight spot is supply still coming.
wrong.Spiking on a wide, heavy down day: That is a heavy down day. It ends the setup before the buy.

questions.q: Is this base contracting?
choices: No; it is wide and loose
Yes; three pullbacks make a VCP
Yes; the dips are shallow
questions.answer: No; it is wide and loose
questions.why: No. A contraction as deep as, or deeper than, the one before ends the idea. These swings are not shrinking.
questions.lesson_line: Equal swings are a box, not a VCP. Wait for the contractions.

wrong.Yes; three pullbacks make a VCP: Three pullbacks only count if they shrink.
wrong.Yes; the dips are shallow: Shallow is fine. The problem is that nothing is contracting.

questions.story: A leader pulls back 14%, rallies, then pulls back another 14%. A third pullback is also about 14%.

questions.q: VCP or flat base?
choices: A VCP
A flat base
A high tight flag
questions.why: A flat base. One box where the swings stay the same size has no real volatility contraction. A VCP's pullbacks shrink one after another.
questions.lesson_line: Same-size swings are a box. Shrinking swings are a VCP.

wrong.A VCP: A VCP needs successive pullbacks that shrink. These do not.
wrong.A high tight flag: A high tight flag needs a near-double first. This is a quiet box.

questions.story: A leader rests six weeks in a 10% range. The swings inside stay about the same size.

questions.q: Which is the VCP?
choices: Both; any tight base is a VCP
The three shrinking pullbacks
Base A, the rounded cup shape
questions.why: The three shrinking pullbacks. A cup is one rounded decline and one handle at the rim. A VCP strings pullbacks that shrink one after another.
questions.lesson_line: Count the pullbacks. A string of shrinking ones is a VCP; one round trip plus a handle is a cup.

wrong.Base A, the rounded cup shape: One round trip plus a handle is a cup, judged by the cup rules.
wrong.Both; any tight base is a VCP: Only a base whose swings keep shrinking is a VCP.

questions.story: Base A is one rounded decline with a small handle at the rim. Base B has three pullbacks, each smaller than the last.

questions.q: Buy or pass?
choices: Buy with a wider stop
Pass; the base has broken
Buy; it cleared the pivot
questions.why: Pass. If the entry day's low is already below the final contraction's low, the base has broken and there is no trade.
questions.lesson_line: The structure comes first. If the day's low breaks the last swing's low, there is no trade.

wrong.Buy; it cleared the pivot: Clearing the pivot is only half the test. The final low must hold.
wrong.Buy with a wider stop: Widening the stop is a named mistake. The structure failed.

questions.story: Price trades through the pivot at 11:00. But the day's low already sits under the final contraction's low.

questions.q: What now?
choices: Add more; it is cheaper
Sell it all at the close
Hold; the stop is the exit
questions.answer: Hold; the stop is the exit
questions.why: Hold. The close back inside the base is the squat, a warning and not an exit by itself. The stop is the exit.
questions.lesson_line: A squat is a warning. Only the stop sells.

wrong.Sell it all at the close: A warning is not an exit. The stop decides.
wrong.Add more; it is cheaper: We never add. One full buy, one stop.

questions.story: You bought the breakout at 28.65. It closes at 28.14, back inside the base, still above your stop.

questions.q: Buy the breakout today?
choices: No; wait until after the report
Yes, but only at half the size
Yes; the setup is a perfect one
questions.answer: No; wait until after the report
questions.why: No. No new buy within 3 trading days before a report. A perfect base does not lift the rule.
questions.lesson_line: Check the report date before every buy. Inside 3 days, wait.

wrong.Yes; the setup is a perfect one: A report is a gap risk the setup cannot see.
wrong.Yes, but only at half the size: The rule bars the new buy, not a size.

questions.story: The final contraction is perfect and price trades through the pivot. The report is in 2 sessions.

questions.q: A close under the 20-day average soon after the breakout is a warning, not an exit.
questions.why: True. A close under the 20-day soon after the breakout is a warning, and so are three lower lows on rising volume. The stop stays the exit.
questions.lesson_line: Warnings tell you to watch. Only the stop sells.

questions.q: What do higher lows mean inside a VCP?
choices: The base drifts under its first low
Each high is below the last high
The last low is above the base low
questions.answer: The last low is above the base low
questions.why: The final low is above the base's lowest low. Kullamagi describes the same orderly look: higher lows and a tightening range.
questions.lesson_line: Each swing's low should lift. The base is building a staircase.

wrong.Each high is below the last high: That describes shrinking highs, not rising lows.
wrong.The base drifts under its first low: A lower low means supply is still coming.

questions.q: Which setup is this?
choices: A VCP in the making
A flat base after a rally
A high tight flag pause
questions.why: A high tight flag. The stock doubled first and paused with no run of shrinking pullbacks. A high tight flag follows a run of 90% or more in 8 weeks or less.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the pole first. A near-double that pauses is a high tight flag.

wrong.A VCP in the making: A VCP shows pullbacks that shrink one after another. This is one quiet pause after a double.
wrong.A flat base after a rally: A flat base follows a smaller run and rests longer.

questions.story: A stock doubles in 7 weeks, then pauses for 18 sessions, 8% deep, with no shrinking pullbacks.

questions.q: Which gate fails?
choices: The second is deeper than the first
The first pullback is too deep
The final contraction is too wide
questions.answer: The final contraction is too wide
questions.why: The final contraction. The rule allows at most 10%, and 12% is too wide to be the tight last swing. This is a loose cup, not a VCP.
questions.lesson_line: The last swing has to be the tightest. 12% is still loose.

wrong.The first pullback is too deep: A 24% first leg is inside the 40% ceiling. The last swing is the problem.
wrong.The second is deeper than the first: It is shallower than the first. The problem is how wide the last swing is.

questions.story: A base has a 24% first pullback and then a 12% second pullback. The 12% pullback is the last one.

questions.q: What is missing?
choices: A dry-up in the last swing's volume
The pivot is too high
The pullbacks are not shrinking
questions.answer: A dry-up in the last swing's volume
questions.why: A dry-up. The final leg traded above the 50-day average volume with no quiet day. The rule needs below 1x and a day at 0.5x or under.
questions.lesson_line: Shrinking swings are not enough. Volume has to dry up too.

wrong.The pullbacks are not shrinking: They shrink from 14% to 4%. That part passes.
wrong.The pivot is too high: The pivot is not the issue. The volume is.

questions.story: Two pullbacks shrink from 14% to 4%. But the final leg traded at 1.13x the 50-day average volume, with no quiet day.

questions.q: What is it really?
choices: A flat base, by Minervini's waiver
A cup with handle
A textbook VCP
questions.answer: A flat base, by Minervini's waiver
questions.why: A flat base. A first contraction of 9.1% is too shallow to contract from. Minervini's waiver says a base under 10% deep needs no contraction.
questions.lesson_line: A base that shallow is already tight. Judge it by the flat base rules.

wrong.A textbook VCP: The first contraction is under the 10% line, so it is not a VCP.
wrong.A cup with handle: There is no rounded decline here. It is a shallow rest.

questions.story: A leader's first pullback is only 9.1% deep. The next one is smaller still, and the stock breaks out.

questions.q: Take it or pass?
choices: Take it, but at half size
Take it; one heavy day is noise
Pass; there is still selling
questions.why: Pass. A heavy-volume down day in the right half ends it before the buy. ChartMill: several heavy down days mean distribution, and you are too early.
questions.lesson_line: A heavy down day on the right side means supply is still coming.

wrong.Take it; one heavy day is noise: The card counts one heavy down day. It is the right-side test.
wrong.Take it, but at half size: Size does not repair a failed gate.

questions.story: A base has tightened nicely. But in the right half, one down day came on 1.6 times the 50-day average volume.

questions.q: Light volume on the breakout day is, by itself, a reason to sell a VCP.
questions.why: False. Light volume raises a red flag, and volume would need to come in soon after, but you maintain your stop regardless.
questions.lesson_line: Light volume is a red flag. The stop is still the exit.

questions.q: Where does the stop go now?
choices: Stay where it was
Under the last swing's low
To breakeven, by default
questions.why: To breakeven by default. The stop moves to breakeven between 2R and 5R, at the first trim by default.
questions.lesson_line: First trim at 3R, and the stop moves to breakeven.

wrong.Under the last swing's low: The stop only moves up, and breakeven is the default after the trim.
wrong.Stay where it was: The rule moves it to breakeven by the first trim.

questions.story: You bought a VCP breakout. It hits 3R, and you sell a third.

questions.q: Which base grades higher on its contractions?
choices: Base A, four contractions
Base B, it is simpler
Both A+; both shrink
questions.why: Base A. Three or four clean contractions, each about half the last, is the A+ picture. Fewer, looser steps grade lower.
questions.lesson_line: A staircase of halves is the A+ picture. Fewer steps grade lower.

wrong.Both A+; both shrink: Both shrink, but the clean run of halves is the A+ picture.
wrong.Base B, it is simpler: Fewer, looser steps are the lower-grade picture.

questions.story: Base A has four contractions: 19%, 8%, 6% and 3.5%. Base B has two contractions: 20% and 14%.

questions.q: Where should the stop have been?
choices: At breakeven
Under the 20-day average
Still at the original stop
questions.why: At the original stop. The breakeven move comes between 2R and 5R, so at 1.18R it had not applied. META then fell back to the stop.
questions.lesson_line: No breakeven before the plan says so. Until then the original stop is the exit.

wrong.At breakeven: The breakeven move is for 2R to 5R, at the first trim.
wrong.Under the 20-day average: A close under the 20-day is a warning, not our stop.

questions.story: META broke out and closed above the pivot. It reached 1.18R, then faded for five sessions and hit the stop.

questions.q: What went wrong?
choices: Nothing; the stop did its job
The base was loose
We should have held through the stop
questions.answer: Nothing; the stop did its job
questions.why: Nothing went wrong. CMG looked like an A grade on its face and still drifted to the stop. It never reached 1R, so our 10-day time stop would have sold it a session sooner. The stop, not an opinion, is the exit.
questions.lesson_line: A clean setup can still lose. The stop is the cost of finding out.

wrong.We should have held through the stop: The stop is the exit. Holding past it is how small losses grow.
wrong.The base was loose: The base passed. The loss came from the market.

questions.story: CMG: two shrinking contractions, 2.0x volume, a close above the pivot. It reached 0.87R, then drifted to the stop 11 sessions later.

questions.q: Account 100,000, risk 0.5%, buy 17.38, stop 16.59. How many shares?
questions.why: 632. Divide the dollars at risk by the risk per share and round down. The shares come from the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Shares come from the stop: risk in dollars divided by risk per share, rounded down.

questions.q: We can build a VCP position in steps as it works.
questions.why: False. The house plan is one full buy at one price with one stop, no pilot buys and no adding.
questions.lesson_line: One full buy, one stop. We do not build in steps.

questions.q: Which average is the default trail for a fast-moving VCP?
choices: The 50-day
The 10-day
The pivot
questions.why: The 10-day for a fast mover, sold on a close below it. A steadier stock can use the 21-day.
questions.lesson_line: Fast mover: trail the 10-day. Steadier: trail the 21-day.

wrong.The 50-day: Too slow for a fast mover; it gives back too much.
wrong.The pivot: The pivot is a level to watch, not a trail.

questions.q: What is the plan?
choices: Sell it and free the money
Add more while it is quiet
Hold; the base was perfect
questions.answer: Sell it and free the money
questions.why: Sell it. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money.
questions.lesson_line: A trade that does nothing for 10 days is sold.

wrong.Hold; the base was perfect: The time stop does not care how good the base was.

questions.story: You bought a VCP breakout 10 trading days ago. It has drifted sideways and is up only 0.5R.

questions.q: What governs the exit?
choices: The first 30-minute low; out past 2R
Keep the old stop and wait it out
Wait for a recovery of the gap
questions.why: The first 30-minute low. On a gap through the stop, that low is the new stop, and past 2R we get out.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop gets the 30-minute rule. Past 2R, get out.

wrong.Wait for a recovery of the gap: The gap rule does not wait. It sets a new stop.
wrong.Keep the old stop and wait it out: The stock is already through it. The gap rule takes over.

questions.story: AXON: the fill was 694.02 and the day's low 691.86, so the stop sat 0.3% under. The next day gapped to 592.76, far through it.

questions.q: Which breakout day reached 3R more often in our scan?
choices: A close above the pivot
No difference at all
A close back inside the base
questions.why: A close above the pivot. In our scan it reached 3R 36.9% of the time against 18.9% for a close back inside the base.
questions.lesson_line: How the breakout day closes matters. Back inside the base is the worst sign.

wrong.A close back inside the base: Those reached 3R about half as often.
wrong.No difference at all: The scan showed a clear gap.

questions.q: What does this tell you?
choices: A strong breakout; volume confirms
A squat; the stop decides
An A+ entry
questions.why: A squat. The breakout cleared 28.64 on 2.3x volume but closed at 28.14, back inside the base. The stop took it the next day.
questions.lesson_line: A volume surge that closes inside the base is a squat. Keep the stop.

wrong.A strong breakout; volume confirms: Volume confirmed nothing; the close gave it all back.
wrong.An A+ entry: A close back inside the base is the warning with the worst numbers.

questions.story: ALGN breaks the pivot on 2.3x volume, then closes at 28.14, back inside the base. The pivot was 28.64.

questions.q: Buy at the pivot?
choices: No; wait for the base high
No; the base is too short
Yes; the pivot is the final swing's high
questions.answer: Yes; the pivot is the final swing's high
questions.why: Yes. The pivot is the final contraction's high, and it may sit below the base's high. JOYY's pivot was 51.22 under a base high of 56.75.
questions.lesson_line: The final swing's high is the pivot, even under the base high.

wrong.No; wait for the base high: Waiting for 56.75 means chasing the move. The pivot is the final swing.
wrong.No; the base is too short: Length is not the problem here.

questions.story: JOYY's base high is 56.75. Its final contraction tops out at 51.22, and the stock trades through 51.22 on heavy volume.

questions.q: What does it do to the grade?
choices: It raises it; a grade cue
It lowers the grade
It voids the setup
questions.answer: It raises it; a grade cue
questions.why: It raises the grade. A last contraction that undercuts a nearby low, recovers, then makes a higher low is a grade cue.
questions.lesson_line: A shakeout that recovers, then a higher low, is a good sign.

wrong.It voids the setup: An undercut that recovers is a cue, not a failure.
wrong.It lowers the grade: A lower low would lower it. This one recovered.

questions.story: The last contraction dips under a nearby low, snaps back the next day, and then forms a higher low.

questions.q: A breakout on light volume. What now?
choices: Add; the quiet is a bargain
Keep the stop and watch for volume
Sell at once; no volume
questions.answer: Keep the stop and watch for volume
questions.why: Keep the stop and watch for volume. Minervini: lack of volume raises a red flag, volume would need to come in soon after, and you maintain your stop regardless.
questions.lesson_line: Light volume is a red flag, not an exit. The stop is the exit.

wrong.Sell at once; no volume: The stop is the exit. Volume is a grade cue.

questions.story: A clean VCP breaks out on 0.7x average volume. It closes above the pivot.

questions.q: What does the base count do to the grade?
choices: Nothing; a clean shape is clean
It grades down; late bases fail
It grades up; the trend is proven
questions.answer: It grades down; late bases fail
questions.why: It grades down. A first or second base has better odds than a third or fourth. Minervini calls a late-stage base obvious to everyone and prone to failure.
questions.lesson_line: A late base grades lower. The first or second base has the better odds.

wrong.Nothing; a clean shape is clean: A clean shape does not fix a late stage.
wrong.It grades up; the trend is proven: A long run makes the base obvious to everyone. That is the risk.

questions.story: A stock is on the fourth base of a two-year run. The pattern looks clean.

questions.q: Was the setup wrong?
choices: Yes; it should have been sold at 1R
Yes; the stop was too tight
No; every gate passed and the stop hit
questions.answer: No; every gate passed and the stop hit
questions.why: No. Every gate passed. A VCP's tight stop sits inside normal noise, and a loss on a correct VCP is the cost of the next winner.
questions.lesson_line: Tight stops get tagged. The loss is planned.

wrong.Yes; it should have been sold at 1R: There is no 1R exit. The trims start at 3R.
wrong.Yes; the stop was too tight: The stop was the honest one.

questions.story: A VCP closes above the pivot near its high, reaches 1.18R, then fades five sessions to the stop.

questions.q: Which warning matters most today?
choices: The first leg; sell at once
The close back under the pivot
Nothing; the volume was fine
questions.answer: The close back under the pivot
questions.why: The close back under the pivot. CRWD closed at 54.18 against a 55.81 pivot on 1.2x volume, with a deep 31.5% first leg. It was stopped in 5 sessions.
questions.lesson_line: Act on the squat the same day: keep the stop, expect a quick answer.

wrong.The first leg; sell at once: The 31.5% first leg is inside the 40% ceiling. The stop decides.
wrong.Nothing; the volume was fine: Volume of 1.2x did not stop the close back inside the base.

questions.story: CRWD's first contraction was 31.5%. On the breakout day it traded through 55.81 but closed at 54.18.

questions.q: Buy or pass?
choices: Buy half size, tight stop
Pass; it is too stretched
Buy; the base is perfect
questions.why: Pass. A long more than 10% above its 10-day average is skipped. Wait for a new setup.
questions.lesson_line: Stretched above the 10-day is a skip, even at the pivot.

wrong.Buy; the base is perfect: The stretch limit applies to every long.
wrong.Buy half size, tight stop: The rule skips the buy, not halves it.

questions.story: A VCP breaks out cleanly. But the stock is 12% above its 10-day average when you find it.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Take it; the pattern is clean
Pass; too thin and too cheap
Take it at half size, tight stop
questions.answer: Pass; too thin and too cheap
questions.why: Pass. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.
questions.lesson_line: The chart comes after the floor.

wrong.Take it at half size, tight stop: Size does not fix a liquidity failure.
wrong.Take it; the pattern is clean: Thin names are not even watched.

questions.story: A tight VCP breaks out on an 8 dollar stock that trades about 5 million dollars a day.

questions.q: Which VCPs do you take?
choices: All three at normal size
None; Orange is Red
Only A+ setups
questions.why: Only A+ setups. Orange means A+ only. Yellow means smaller and fewer.
questions.lesson_line: Orange: A+ only. Yellow: smaller and fewer. Red: none.

wrong.None; Orange is Red: Red is no VCP buys. Orange allows A+ only.

questions.story: Your market reading turns Orange. Three VCPs set up. One is A+, two are B grade.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Pass; it is not a leader by our rule
Take it at half size, weak group
Take it; Minervini's floor is 70
questions.answer: Pass; it is not a leader by our rule
questions.why: Pass. We buy leaders, with an RS rating of 80 or more in a strong group. An RS of 72 in a weak group is not that.
questions.lesson_line: Buy leaders. A tight chart on a laggard waits.

wrong.Take it; Minervini's floor is 70: The house rule is stricter than his floor.
wrong.Take it at half size, weak group: Size does not fix a leadership gap.

questions.story: A clean VCP sets up in a lone stock in a weak group. Its RS rating is 72.

questions.q: What happens to the setup?
choices: It is fine; one close is just noise
It is fine; the base is still tight
It is off until the trend recovers
questions.answer: It is off until the trend recovers
questions.why: It is off. A close under the 200-day, or a failed Trend Template line, ends the setup before the buy.
questions.lesson_line: Lose the trend and the base is off. Check the trend again before the buy.

wrong.It is fine; the base is still tight: The trend check outranks the box.
wrong.It is fine; one close is just noise: A close under the 200-day ends it before the buy.

questions.story: A base is forming nicely. Then the stock closes below its 200-day average.

questions.q: What happens to the count?
choices: Move the stop lower
Buy anyway at the old pivot
It starts again
questions.why: It starts again. A close below the final contraction's low ends that pivot, and a new tight contraction makes a new pivot.
questions.lesson_line: Close under the last low and the count restarts.

wrong.Buy anyway at the old pivot: The structure broke. The old pivot is gone.
wrong.Move the stop lower: The stop never moves down or wider.

questions.story: Before you buy, the stock closes below the low of its final contraction.

questions.q: A base whose first pullback was 55% can still be a VCP.
questions.why: False. A first contraction over 40%, or any fall of 60% or more, ends it. A fall that deep is failure prone.
questions.lesson_line: A first leg that deep means too much damage. Pass.

questions.q: How big is the position?
choices: 50% of the account
20% of the account
40% of the account
questions.why: 40% of the account. A 1% risk on a 2% stop is 50% of the account, capped to 40% by the position cap.
questions.lesson_line: A tight stop can ask for a huge size. The cap holds it at 40%.

wrong.50% of the account: The size is the smaller of the risk-based size and the cap.
wrong.20% of the account: The rule caps a position at 40%, not 20%.

questions.story: Account 100,000. You risk 1% on a stop 2% under the entry. The risk-based size is 50% of the account.

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before a breakout. Do the pullbacks shrink and does volume dry up? Take it or pass.
choices: Pass; the first swing is too deep
Take it; swings and volume shrink
Pass; the swings are about equal
questions.answer: Take it; swings and volume shrink
questions.why: Take it. Contractions of 16.6%, 11.0% and 3.5%, a final swing riding the 10-day at 0.46x the average volume. It broke out next day on 2.4x volume.
questions.lesson_line: Count the swings and check the volume before you look at the breakout.

wrong.Pass; the swings are about equal: They shrink: the last is far smaller than the first.

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before it trades through its pivot. Does volume dry up in the final leg? Take it or pass.
choices: Pass; no dry-up in the final leg
Take it; the swings keep shrinking
Take it; the base is long enough
questions.answer: Pass; no dry-up in the final leg
questions.why: Pass. The pullbacks shrink, 14% then 4%, but the final leg traded above the 50-day average volume with no quiet day.
questions.lesson_line: Shrinking price is not enough. Look at the volume bars in the last swing.

wrong.Take it; the swings keep shrinking: They do shrink, but the dry-up test failed.
wrong.Take it; the base is long enough: Length does not replace the dry-up.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Check the base and stop first
Buy half and set a stop later
Buy now before it runs away
questions.answer: Check the base and stop first
questions.why: Check it yourself. Never take a trade from an alert, a post or a video without your own entry, stop and size.
questions.lesson_line: Someone else's alert is not a plan. Build your own entry, stop and size.

wrong.Buy now before it runs away: A buy with no stop and no size is a gamble.
wrong.Buy half and set a stop later: Half a gamble is still a gamble.

questions.story: A video says a stock is breaking out of a VCP right now. You have not looked at its base, stop or size.

questions.q: What is your call?
choices: Buy it; the stock is a leader
Pass; Red means no VCP buys
Buy a starter
questions.answer: Pass; Red means no VCP buys
questions.why: Pass. Red means no VCP buys. Even perfect VCPs fail en masse when buyers are missing.
questions.lesson_line: A great setup in a Red market waits. Cash is a position.

wrong.Buy a starter: A starter in a Red market is still a long.
wrong.Buy it; the stock is a leader: Leadership does not cancel a Red market.

questions.story: A textbook VCP is one tick from its pivot. The market reading is Red.

questions.q: Which base is cleaner?
choices: Base A: selling shakes out weak hands
Base B: a quiet right side
Neither; volume does not matter
questions.answer: Base B: a quiet right side
questions.why: Base B. If price and volume do not quiet down on the right side, supply is still coming. A heavy down day in the right half ends the setup.
questions.lesson_line: A quiet right side is the clean one.

wrong.Base A: selling shakes out weak hands: Heavy selling on the right side is distribution.
wrong.Neither; volume does not matter: The right-side test is a gate.

questions.story: Two bases have the same three shrinking swings. In Base A one right-half down day came on heavy volume. Base B's right half is quiet.

questions.q: How does the location grade the setup?
choices: They grade the same on shape alone
A pivot near the high grades up
Base B; the room above is bigger
questions.answer: A pivot near the high grades up
questions.why: A pivot at or near a 52-week or all-time high, with no overhead supply, is the A+ picture. A pivot well below the left-side high is B-.
questions.lesson_line: No overhead supply is the best location.

wrong.Base B; the room above is bigger: Overhead supply sits above Base B's pivot.

questions.story: Two VCPs have the same shape. Base A's pivot sits at an all-time high. Base B's pivot sits well below its left-side high.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Wait; one full buy at the trigger
Buy half now
Buy all now at a tight stop
questions.answer: Wait; one full buy at the trigger
questions.why: Wait for the trigger. The plan is one full buy at one price with one stop, no pilot buys. Buying early in the base is a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: No pilot buys. We buy the trigger, not the dream.

wrong.Buy half now: A pilot buy is not allowed.
wrong.Buy all now at a tight stop: Buying before the pivot breaks is a named mistake.

questions.story: A VCP is two days from its pivot. A friend says to buy half now and the other half at the breakout.

questions.q: What do you do about the stop?
choices: Widen the stop to give it room
Keep the stop; cut size or skip
Pull the stop in to fit the size
questions.answer: Keep the stop; cut size or skip
questions.why: Keep the honest stop. If it does not fit the risk, shrink the size or skip. Widening the stop to give the stock room is a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: The stop does not bend to fit the size. The size bends to the stop.

wrong.Widen the stop to give it room: The stop only moves up, never wider.
wrong.Pull the stop in to fit the size: Pulling the stop in to fit the size is a trap.

questions.story: The honest stop is wider than you like. A friend says to give it even more room.

questions.q: For a VCP we prefer growing sales and earnings, but the chart comes first.
questions.why: True. We prefer a company with growing sales and earnings. The chart still comes first.
questions.lesson_line: Fundamentals are a plus. The chart comes first.

questions.q: What does our rule say about the buy?
choices: The chart comes first; pass
The earnings come first; buy it
Both count the same; buy half size
questions.why: Pass. Growing sales and earnings are preferred, but the chart comes first. This base is not contracting.
questions.lesson_line: Strong earnings do not fix a loose chart. The chart comes first.

wrong.The earnings come first; buy it: Earnings are a preference. They do not replace the chart rules.
wrong.Both count the same; buy half size: The chart comes first, so they do not count the same. A base that is not contracting is not a VCP.

questions.story: A company posts fast sales and earnings growth. Its base is wide and loose, and the pullbacks are not shrinking.

questions.q: A down day in the second half of a base trades 3,300,000 shares. The 50-day average is 2,200,000. How many times the average?
questions.why: 1.5. That meets our limit of 1.5 times the 50-day average, so this base still has selling on its right side.
questions.lesson_line: A down day at 1.5 times the average or more on the right side is selling.

questions.q: A down day on 1.5 times the 50-day volume in the base's second half is fine if shallow.
questions.why: False. Our card wants no down day in the second half on 1.5 times the 50-day volume or more, however shallow.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy down days on the right side mean distribution is still going on.

questions.q: Which base grades higher on the closes?
choices: Base A, the closes are tight
Base B, a wider range of closes
Neither; only the depth matters
questions.answer: Base A, the closes are tight
questions.why: Base A. Tight closes, with little change from one day to the next, are a grade cue in the final contraction.
questions.lesson_line: In the final contraction, tight closes day to day and week to week grade higher.

wrong.Base B, a wider range of closes: Loose closes grade lower. The cue is little change from one day to the next.
wrong.Neither; only the depth matters: Both are 5% deep, so the closes decide. The card grades on tight closes too.

questions.story: Two bases end in a 5% final contraction on quiet volume. In base A the closes sit within a few cents day to day. In base B they jump around inside the range.

questions.q: Tight closes in the final contraction are a grade cue for a VCP, not a gate.
questions.why: True. Our card calls it a grade cue: tight closes with little change from one day to the next.
questions.lesson_line: Tight closes make a final contraction grade higher.

questions.q: What did the plan miss?
choices: A live stop order with the broker
A wider stop to ride the shakeout
A smaller buy, spread over two days
questions.answer: A live stop order with the broker
questions.why: A live stop order with the broker. Our rule is an order in place, not a stop kept in your head or your notes.
questions.lesson_line: A stop in your notes is not a stop. Put the order in with the broker.

wrong.A wider stop to ride the shakeout: A stop never goes wider. The problem was that no order existed.
wrong.A smaller buy, spread over two days: We do not build a VCP in steps; it is one full buy. The missing piece was the order.

questions.story: You buy a VCP breakout at 17.38 and write the stop, 16.59, in your notes. No order is placed. At 11 am the stock trades 16.20 while you are in a meeting.

questions.q: Watching the stop on your screen all day is as good as a stop order with the broker.
questions.why: False. Our rule is a real order with the broker. An eye on the screen is not an order.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is an order, not a habit of watching.

questions.q: You bought 900 shares. You sell a third of them at 3R and another third at 5R. How many are left to trail?
questions.why: 300. A third at 3R and a third at 5R leaves the last third, which is trailed.
questions.lesson_line: Thirds at 3R and 5R, then trail the last third.

questions.q: What does the plan do at 5R?
choices: Sell a third more; trail the rest
Sell everything and lock the gain in
Hold it all until the 21-day breaks
questions.answer: Sell a third more; trail the rest
questions.why: Sell another third. After the first third at 3R comes a third at 5R, then the last third is trailed.
questions.lesson_line: Third at 3R, third at 5R, trail the last third.

wrong.Sell everything and lock the gain in: The plan sells in thirds and trails the last one.
wrong.Hold it all until the 21-day breaks: The second third comes off at 5R. Only the last third rides the trail.

questions.story: Your VCP buy sold its first third at 3R. Price now touches 5R and the stop is at breakeven.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A trim level the VCP gaps over is taken at the ___.
questions.why: Open. If a stock opens above a trim level, 3R or 5R, take that trim at the open.
questions.lesson_line: If it gaps over your trim level, take the trim at the open.

questions.q: How do you handle the second trim?
choices: Take the trim at the open
Wait for it to dip back to 21.40
Skip the trim and raise the stop
questions.answer: Take the trim at the open
questions.why: Take the trim at the open. If a stock opens above a trim level, we take that trim there.
questions.lesson_line: When a stock gaps over a trim level, the trim comes off at the open.

wrong.Wait for it to dip back to 21.40: The level is passed. The rule takes the trim at the open.
wrong.Skip the trim and raise the stop: The plan has no skipped trims. The level was passed, so the trim comes off at the open.

questions.story: Your VCP buy has its 5R level at 21.40. The first third came off at 3R. The stock gaps up and opens at 22.10.

questions.q: What do you do with the position?
choices: Sell a big part into the burst
Add, since the leg is strong
Hold it all until the trail breaks
questions.answer: Sell a big part into the burst
questions.why: Sell a big part into the burst. On a climax run in your own long, how much to sell is a judgment call.
questions.lesson_line: Into a climax run, sell a big part. How much is your call.

wrong.Add, since the leg is strong: No adds. A climax is where we sell, not where we buy more.
wrong.Hold it all until the trail breaks: The rule is to sell a big part into a climax, not to wait for the trail.
